title: The Metropolis Engine: Mechanics & Calibration
text:
Code
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

source("R/metropolis_sampler.R")
source("R/plots.R")

# Target: Correlated bivariate normal
target_toy <- function(theta) {
  mu <- c(0, 0)
  sigma <- matrix(c(1.0, 0.75, 0.75, 1.0), nrow = 2)
  -0.5 * t(theta - mu) %*% solve(sigma) %*% (theta - mu)
}

# Run 3 chains with varying step sizes to demonstrate tuning
chain_timid <- run_metropolis(target_toy, initial_theta = c(0, 0), iterations = 2000, proposal_sd = 0.03, seed = 101)
chain_wild  <- run_metropolis(target_toy, initial_theta = c(0, 0), iterations = 2000, proposal_sd = 3.20, seed = 101)
chain_tuned <- run_metropolis(target_toy, initial_theta = c(0, 0), iterations = 2000, proposal_sd = 1.20, seed = 101)


he Four Steps of Metropolis-Hastings Rather than solving high-dimensional integrals analytically, the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm generates samples from an unnormalized target density via four iterative steps:  1. Propose a Candidate Move: Given the current state ‭\(\theta^{(t)}\)‬, sample candidate coordinates ‭\(\theta^*\)‬ from a symmetric proposal distribution: ‭\[\theta^* \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\theta^{(t)}, \sigma_{\epsilon}^2 \mathbf{I}\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬ 2. Evaluate the Hastings Acceptance Ratio (‭\(\alpha\)‬): Compare target density at the candidate position to the current state: ‭\[\alpha = \min\left(1, \frac{p(\theta^*)}{p(\theta^{(t)})}\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬ In practice, this is evaluated in log-space to prevent numerical floating-point underflow: ‭\[\log \alpha = \min\left(0, \log p(\theta^*) - \log p(\theta^{(t)})\right)\]‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ 3. The Acceptance Decision: Draw a uniform scalar ‭\(u \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 1)\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬. If ‭\(\log u < \log \alpha\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬, the candidate is accepted: ‭\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^*\]‬‭‬ Otherwise, the candidate is rejected, and the chain remains in place: ‭\[\theta^{(t+1)} = \theta^{(t)}\]‬‭‬ > Note: While occasionally accepting lower-density moves enables traversal across non-convex surfaces, standard Random-Walk Metropolis remains vulnerable to getting trapped between separated modes on complex, multimodal target surfaces.  4. Iterate: Repeating this transition rule generates an empirical chain whose visited states converge asymptotically to the target posterior distribution ‭\(p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬.


The Complete Engine in Pure R
Below is the complete sampling engine implemented from first principles in base R:


Code
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)

run_metropolis <- function(target_log_posterior,
                           initial_theta,
                           iterations = 5000,
                           proposal_sd = 0.05,
                           seed = NULL) {
  if (!is.null(seed)) set.seed(seed)

  d <- length(initial_theta)
  theta_current <- initial_theta
  log_p_current <- target_log_posterior(theta_current)

  draws_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = iterations, ncol = d)
  accepted  <- logical(iterations)
  log_probs <- numeric(iterations)

  for (t in 1:iterations) {
    if (is.matrix(proposal_sd)) {
      theta_candidate <- MASS::mvrnorm(1, mu = theta_current, Sigma = proposal_sd)
    } else {
      theta_candidate <- rnorm(d, mean = theta_current, sd = proposal_sd)
    }

    log_p_candidate <- target_log_posterior(theta_candidate)
    log_alpha <- log_p_candidate - log_p_current

    if (!is.na(log_alpha) && log(runif(1)) < log_alpha) {
      theta_current <- theta_candidate
      log_p_current <- log_p_candidate
      accepted[t]   <- TRUE
    } else {
      accepted[t]   <- FALSE
    }

    draws_mat[t, ] <- theta_current
    log_probs[t]   <- log_p_current
  }

  param_names <- if (!is.null(names(initial_theta))) {
    names(initial_theta)
  } else {
    paste0("theta_", seq_len(d))
  }

  draws_df <- as_tibble(draws_mat, .name_repair = "minimal")
  colnames(draws_df) <- param_names
  draws_df <- draws_df %>% mutate(iteration = seq_len(iterations))

  diagnostics_df <- tibble(
    iteration = seq_len(iterations),
    accepted = accepted,
    log_posterior = log_probs
  )

  list(
    draws = draws_df,
    acceptance_rate = mean(accepted),
    diagnostics = diagnostics_df,
    dimensions = d,
    proposal_sd = proposal_sd
  )
}





The Step-Size Dilemma: Tuning Proposal Variance
The primary operational lever in Random-Walk Metropolis is the proposal standard deviation (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon}\)‬). Tuning this parameter governs the trade-off between spatial displacement per jump and proposal rejection frequency:


Code
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

plot_step_size_comparison(chain_timid, chain_wild, chain_tuned)





Figure 1: Trace plots illustrating the impact of proposal step size on chain mixing and acceptance




Understanding the Trace Plots
The trace panels illustrate the trajectory of parameter ‭\(\theta_1\)‬ over 2,000 steps under three distinct proposal step sizes (‭\(\sigma_\epsilon\)‬), showing how proposal variance governs chain exploration:

Too Timid (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 0.03\)‬‭‬ — Bottom Panel): Almost every proposal is accepted (98.5% acceptance), but displacement per step is small. The chain wanders sluggishly through diffusion rather than stationary mixing, exhibiting strong positive autocorrelation and requiring extensive iterations to traverse the distribution.
Too Aggressive (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 3.20\)‬‭‬ — Middle Panel): Large proposal jumps land frequently in low-probability density tails, leading to a rejection rate exceeding 90% (9.9% acceptance). The trace exhibits horizontal flatlines where the state remains frozen across multiple consecutive iterations.
Calibrated (‭\(\sigma_{\epsilon} = 1.20\)‬‭‬ — Top Panel): Jump radius is balanced against target density gradients, achieving an empirical acceptance rate of approximately 34.2% (aligning with theoretical targets of 25% to 40% for low dimensions). The trajectory rapidly oscillates across the distribution center. However, while a calibrated acceptance rate is necessary, it does not alone guarantee rapid autocorrelation decay when applied to high-dimensional, correlated parameters.

title: The Mechanics of Markov Chain Monte Carlo
text:
Introduction
Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is a computational class of algorithms designed to sample from complex, high-dimensional probability distributions when analytical integration is intractable. In portfolio risk management, evaluating joint risk across multiple assets requires characterizing dependent parameters simultaneously—including factor means, volatilities, and cross-asset correlations. For non-standard priors or complex likelihoods, deterministic numerical grid integration scales exponentially with dimension (‭\(K^D\)‬), quickly exceeding practical computational limits.
MCMC bypasses deterministic grid mapping by replacing brute-force evaluation with an informed random walk. Guided by transition rules such as the Metropolis-Hastings criterion, the sampler proposes local moves, accepting higher-density coordinates and probabilistically accepting lower-density proposals. Over extended sampling runs, the chain visits parameter states in proportion to their underlying posterior density, mapping the target space without evaluating intractable normalizing constants.
In this demonstration, we focus on isolating parameter estimation uncertainty. Using a controlled multivariate Gaussian portfolio framework, we deliberately pair our pure-R Metropolis sampler against a model with an exact analytical solution: ‭\(\boldsymbol{\mu} \mid \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{\Sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar{\mathbf{x}}, \frac{1}{n}\mathbf{\Sigma})\)‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬‭‬. By holding covariance fixed and evaluating expected returns against this closed-form baseline, we provide an auditable environment to examine convergence, proposal efficiency, and the propagation of parameter uncertainty into Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES).



Plain-Language Translation: How It Works
Imagine being placed on a large, pitch-black terrain with only a small flashlight, tasked with mapping the highest peaks and ridges. You cannot view the entire landscape at once, and pacing every square foot on a rigid grid would take an impractical amount of time. Instead, you take incremental random steps. When a step leads uphill toward higher ground, you take it; when a step heads downhill, you occasionally take it anyway to avoid staying confined to a single minor hill. Because you spend most of your time traversing higher ridges and pass quickly through low valleys, your path naturally traces the contours of the landscape. In financial modeling, algorithms like Markov Chain Monte Carlo deploy this sequential exploration to estimate portfolio risk. Rather than evaluating billions of arbitrary grid points across multiple correlated factors, the sampler concentrates computational effort directly in regions of high probability.



The Dimensional Scaling Challenge
When managing risk across multiple correlated factors—equity betas, credit spreads, duration, and commodities—quantifying joint parameter uncertainty is essential. In low dimensions, deterministic numerical quadratures or grid evaluations are trivial. However, as the parameter count (‭\(D\)‬) increases, Cartesian grid evaluations scale exponentially (‭\(K^D\)‬).

generate_dimension_comparison() %>%
  gt() %>%

    title = md("**Dimensional Complexity: Grid Search vs. Stochastic Sampling**"),

Low-Dimensional Space (‭\(D = 2\)‬‭‬): A coarse 10-point grid requires only ‭\(10^2 = 100\)‬‭‬ function evaluations, making numerical quadratures instantaneous.
Moderate Parameter Space (‭\(D = 10\)‬‭‬): Uniform evaluation along each axis requires ‭\(10^{10}\)‬ calculations (10 billion operations)—creating significant runtime bottlenecks in standard computing environments, whereas stochastic sampling traverses the distribution in seconds.
Full Covariance Horizon (‭\(D = 20\)‬‭‬): Modeling 20 factor means alongside full cross-asset covariances involves ‭\(D + D(D+1)/2 = 230\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ distinct parameters. Evaluating such spaces on uniform deterministic grids is computationally intractable, making stochastic simulation essential for non-conjugate structures.



The Random Walk Engine
Markov Chain Monte Carlo navigates probability distributions via sequential, localized transitions:

Propose a Move: The chain samples a candidate coordinate ‭\(\theta^*\)‬ from a proposal distribution centered on the current state ‭\(\theta^{(t)}\)‬.
Evaluate Density Ratio: It computes the target posterior probability ratio between candidate and current locations.
Accept or Reject: Proposals into higher-density regions are accepted; lower-density moves are accepted probabilistically, enabling the chain to explore parameter tails.







NoteThe Metropolis-Hastings Random Walk



Evaluating joint portfolio risk across multiple interdependent assets presents substantial computational complexity when models deviate from simple analytical assumptions. Calculating every joint market permutation across a fine grid requires billions of evaluations, creating an operational bottleneck. The Metropolis-Hastings algorithm resolves this by deploying a sequential “digital scout.” Rather than attempting to evaluate the entire parameter space uniformly, the algorithm takes incremental steps through potential states. If a proposed move discovers a region of higher probability, the chain transitions there; if it steps toward a lower-probability scenario, it still accepts the move occasionally to ensure thorough exploration. Over thousands of iterations, the algorithm visits parameter combinations in proportion to their joint posterior probability. This produces an empirical distribution of parameter uncertainty. For executive decision-makers, this turns otherwise intractable high-dimensional estimation into a practical sampling process, providing an empirical baseline for setting risk capital and stress limits.




Code
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 10

plot_random_walk_2d(hero_chain$draws, n_steps = 180)





Figure 1: Metropolis-Hastings chain traversing a correlated bivariate parameter space.





Traversal Mechanics

Stationary Convergence: Initializing from an arbitrary coordinate in the outer tail, the chain transitions toward the high-density contour core.
Proportional Dwell Time: Once stationary, the chain continues moving, spending time across regions in proportion to target posterior density.





Project Structure & Roadmap
This project demonstrates the implementation, diagnostic auditing, and tail-risk application of first-principles MCMC:

The Metropolis Engine: The R implementation from scratch (without MCMC libraries), detailing acceptance ratios and proposal step-size calibration.
Portfolio Risk Model: Sampling the 10-factor posterior under fixed covariance to evaluate Value at Risk (VaR) and Expected Shortfall (ES), benchmarked against the exact closed-form posterior.
Audit & Diagnostics: Four-chain convergence checks with split-\(\hat{R}\), autocorrelation decay, and Effective Sample Size (ESS) audits cross-checked against the posterior package.

title: 10-Factor Portfolio Risk & Tail Estimation
text:
Introduction
This chapter transitions from two-dimensional toy mechanics to a multi-asset portfolio comprising ten correlated risk factor exposures—spanning core equity betas, corporate credit carry, duration hedges, and commodities.
To provide a mathematically rigorous audit baseline, we formulate a Bayesian return model with a known closed-form solution. We model daily returns as multivariate normal \(\mathbf{R} \sim \mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{\Sigma})\) with a diffuse Gaussian prior on the mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, 10^3 \mathbf{I})\) and condition the covariance matrix on the empirical sample estimate \(\mathbf{\Sigma} = \hat{\mathbf{\Sigma}}_{\text{emp}}\). Under this conjugate structure, the joint posterior distribution of expected returns is analytically known: \[\boldsymbol{\mu} \mid \mathbf{R}, \mathbf{\Sigma} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(\bar{\mathbf{x}}, \frac{1}{n} \mathbf{\Sigma}\right)\]
While a closed-form solution exists for this specific Gaussian model, using it as our target allows us to directly benchmark MCMC performance. We can compare the empirical draws, standard errors, and credible intervals from our first-principles Metropolis sampler directly against the analytical truth.


Code
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

library(dplyr)
library(gt)
library(scales)
library(ggplot2)

source("R/metropolis_sampler.R")
source("R/risk_functions.R")
source("R/plots.R")

# 1. Ingest synthetic book fixture and build log-posterior
model_fixture <- build_risk_target("data/synthetic_returns.csv")

# 2. Run 10-dimensional MCMC chain
init_theta <- rep(0, model_fixture$d)
names(init_theta) <- model_fixture$asset_names

chain_10d <- run_metropolis(
  target_log_posterior = model_fixture$target_fn,
  initial_theta = init_theta,
  iterations = 3000,
  proposal_sd = 0.00032,
  seed = 42
)

# 3. Discard first 500 draws as burn-in
post_burn_draws <- chain_10d$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500)

# 4. Tail risk evaluation across equal-weighted portfolio
weights_eq <- rep(0.10, 10)
risk_table <- evaluate_portfolio_tail_risk(
  draws_df = post_burn_draws,
  weights = weights_eq,
  cov_mat = model_fixture$cov_emp,
  alpha = 0.95
)

# 5. Pre-formatted text variables for dynamic inline reporting
acc_rate_txt   <- sprintf("%.1f%%", chain_10d$acceptance_rate * 100)
var_mean_txt   <- sprintf("%.2f%%", risk_table$mean_estimate[1] * 100)
var_ci_txt     <- sprintf("[%.2f%%, %.2f%%]", risk_table$ci_05[1] * 100, risk_table$ci_95[1] * 100)
es_mean_txt    <- sprintf("%.2f%%", risk_table$mean_estimate[2] * 100)
es_ci_txt      <- sprintf("[%.2f%%, %.2f%%]", risk_table$ci_05[2] * 100, risk_table$ci_95[2] * 100)
n_draws_txt    <- comma(nrow(post_burn_draws))




Sampling the 10-Factor Joint Posterior
The sampler processes 250 trading days of observed returns across all 10 assets simultaneously. Starting cold at ‭\(\boldsymbol{\mu}_0 = \mathbf{0}\)‬‭‬, the chain completes 3,000 iterations, discarding the first 500 iterations to eliminate initialization bias. The chain operates at an empirical acceptance rate of 28.9%.


Code
risk_table %>%
  gt() %>%
  tab_header(
    title = md("**10-Asset Portfolio Tail Risk Estimates (1-Day Horizon)**"),
    subtitle = "Posterior mean risk metrics and 90% Bayesian credible intervals under parameter uncertainty"
  ) %>%
  cols_label(
    metric = "Tail Risk Measure",
    mean_estimate = "Posterior Mean",
    ci_05 = "5th Percentile",
    ci_95 = "95th Percentile"
  ) %>%
  fmt_percent(columns = c(mean_estimate, ci_05, ci_95), decimals = 2) %>%
  tab_options(table.font.size = 12)

Context: Isolating Parameter Risk in the Mean Vector
Because the return distribution is modeled as multivariate normal and ‭\(\mathbf{\Sigma}\)‬ is fixed at the sample estimate, the portfolio tail metrics reflect the properties of Gaussian loss distributions under estimation uncertainty:

Mean Uncertainty Bounds (‭\(\text{VaR}_{95\%}\)‬): For an equal-weighted portfolio, parametric Value at Risk is governed by ‭\(\text{VaR}_{95\%} \approx -\mathbf{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu} + 1.645 \cdot \sigma_p\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬‭‬. Because covariance is held constant, the 12 basis point spread between the 5th and 95th percentiles (‭\(0.99\%\)‬‭‬ to ‭\(1.11\%\)‬‭‬) reflects the estimation uncertainty of the portfolio mean alone (‭\(\pm 1.645 \cdot \sigma_p / \sqrt{n}\)‬‭‬‭‬), setting aside covariance uncertainty.
Expected Shortfall Ratio (‭\(\text{ES}_{95\%}\)‬): The ratio of Expected Shortfall to Value at Risk (‭\(1.33\% / 1.05\% \approx 1.27\)‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬ ‭‬) reflects standard Gaussian tail expectation constants (‭\(\approx 2.063 / 1.645\)‬‭‬), adjusted for the portfolio drift. Under a normal likelihood, this metric captures linear downside expectation rather than excess kurtosis or heavy-tailed structural shocks.




Benchmarking MCMC Against the Exact Posterior
Because this model is conjugate, the exact posterior is known. With the diffuse prior \(\boldsymbol{\mu} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, 10^3\mathbf{I})\), the posterior is Gaussian with covariance \(\mathbf{V} = (n\hat{\Sigma}^{-1} + 10{-3}\mathbf{I}){-1}\). Portfolio VaR and ES are linear in \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\), so their exact posteriors are also normal. That lets us check every MCMC output against the true answer.

What the Benchmark Shows
The MCMC point estimates match the exact posterior: portfolio VaR and ES means agree to the second decimal place. The credible intervals are narrower than they should be. The MCMC VaR interval is about 83% of the exact width, so the sampler understates parameter uncertainty.
The per-factor table shows where this comes from. Factors with the slowest mixing (lowest ESS on the Audit & Diagnostics page) show the largest SD shortfall and the largest mean error. With only 19–122 effective draws, the chain has not explored the posterior tails fully.
Implication for risk reporting: a poorly mixed sampler can report the right central estimate while producing credible intervals that are too narrow, which understates parameter risk. Without a closed-form benchmark or proper diagnostics, this failure would go unnoticed.
Parameter Distributions vs. Generative Ground Truth
Because the fixture was simulated from known parameters, we can compare the sampled MCMC distributions against both the generative population values and the analytical sample estimates.


Code
plot_posterior_marginals(
  draws_df = post_burn_draws,
  asset_name = "Tech_Growth",
  true_val = 0.110 / 252
)





Figure 1: Marginal posterior distribution for Tech Growth expected daily returns.






Code
plot_posterior_marginals(
  draws_df = post_burn_draws,
  asset_name = "US_Treas_10Y",
  true_val = 0.035 / 252
)





Figure 2: Marginal posterior distribution for 10Y US Treasury returns(Duration hedge).




Understanding the Marginal Density Plots
Tech Growth: The posterior centers on the sample mean, approximately 0.34% daily, with a posterior standard deviation of about 0.10%. The 90% credible interval runs from +0.17% to +0.47%. The true value used to generate the data, +0.044% daily (+11.0% annualized), lies about 2.8 posterior standard deviations below the center.
This is not a sampler error. By chance, this 250-day sample shows a Tech Growth drift of roughly 82% annualized. The posterior correctly reports what the data support; the data simply don’t support the true value.
US Treasuries (10Y): The posterior centers near -0.02% daily, with a standard deviation of about +0.03% and a 90% credible interval of -0.07% to +0.03%. The true value (+0.014% daily) lies about 1.1 standard deviations from the center.
Narrowing Tech Growth’s uncertainty to 0.01% daily would take about 25,451 trading days of data.






ImportantKey Takeaway: Parameter Recovery Is a Data Problem, Not a Sampler Problem



MCMC recovers the posterior, not the truth. With 250 daily observations, mean returns are poorly identified: Tech Growth’s posterior standard deviation (≈0.10% daily) is more than twice its true mean. Narrowing that uncertainty to about 0.01% daily would take roughly  25,451 trading days of data. For risk managers, a year of history can’t reliably tell a high-drift asset from a low-drift one. That estimation uncertainty is exactly what the VaR and ES credible intervals are meant to capture.

title: Audit & Diagnostics
text:
Code
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(posterior)
library(reactable)
library(scales)
library(tidyverse)

source("R/metropolis_sampler.R")
source("R/risk_functions.R")
source("R/plots.R")
source("R/diagnostics.R")

# 1. Ingest fixture and run two independent chains to test mixing
model_fixture <- build_risk_target("data/synthetic_returns.csv")
d <- model_fixture$d
asset_names <- model_fixture$asset_names

init_theta1 <- rep(0, d)
names(init_theta1) <- asset_names

init_theta2 <- rep(0.001, d)
names(init_theta2) <- asset_names

chain1 <- run_metropolis(
  target_log_posterior = model_fixture$target_fn,
  initial_theta = init_theta1,
  iterations = 3000,
  proposal_sd = 0.00032,
  seed = 42
)

n_obs       <- nrow(model_fixture$returns_mat)
post_center <- colMeans(model_fixture$returns_mat)
post_sd     <- sqrt(diag(model_fixture$cov_emp) / n_obs)

set.seed(2026)
signs <- sample(c(-1, 1), d, replace = TRUE)
starts <- list(
  post_center + 3 * post_sd,          # all high
  post_center - 3 * post_sd,          # all low
  post_center + 3 * post_sd * signs   # mixed
)
seeds <- c(99, 123, 456)

extra_chains <- lapply(seq_along(starts), function(i) {
  th <- starts[[i]]; names(th) <- asset_names
  run_metropolis(model_fixture$target_fn, th,
                 iterations = 3000, proposal_sd = 0.00032, seed = seeds[i])
})

all_chains <- c(list(chain1), extra_chains)
chain2 <- extra_chains[[1]]   # keeps txt_acc_c2 working

# Burn-in discard (first 500 draws)
draws_clean  <- lapply(all_chains, function(ch) ch$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500))
draws1_clean <- draws_clean[[1]]

# Burn-in discard (first 500 draws)
draws1_clean <- chain1$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500)
## draws2_clean <- chain2$draws %>% slice_tail(n = 2500)

# 2. Effective Sample Size (Geyer initial monotone sequence; see R/diagnostics.R)
ess_tech  <- compute_ess_robust(draws1_clean$Tech_Growth)
ess_treas <- compute_ess_robust(draws1_clean$US_Treas_10Y)
ess_large <- compute_ess_robust(draws1_clean$US_LargeCap)

Introduction
In institutional risk management, stochastic simulation models must be transparent and auditable. When using Markov Chain Monte Carlo to evaluate high-dimensional portfolio distributions, point estimates alone are insufficient. Because MCMC generates a sequence of dependent parameter proposals rather than independent samples, model validation requires empirical verification of convergence, parameter space exploration, and statistical sample efficiency.
This audit page examines the algorithmic health checks for the 10-dimensional Gaussian random walk. We evaluate multi-chain convergence, measure autocorrelation decay across factor lags, and apply Geyer’s initial sequence estimator to compute robust Effective Sample Size (ESS). This diagnostic audit outlines both the utility of Random-Walk Metropolis and the operational limitations encountered when isotropic proposals are applied to correlated factor distributions.


Dataset Architecture & Methodological Rationale
The analysis utilizes a fixed synthetic fixture of 250 trading days across 10 correlated asset classes (data/synthetic_returns.csv), generated from a known multivariate normal distribution ‭\(\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{\Sigma})\)‬‭‬‭‬‭‬ ‭‬‭‬ calibrated to realistic risk levels: annualized returns between 3.5% and 11.0%, volatilities between 8.0% and 26.0%, and correlations from -0.30 to +0.78.
Using a synthetic baseline provides a controlled ground truth. In empirical market feeds, true data-generating distributions are obscured by regime shifts, structural breaks, and survivorship bias. By defining a synthetic population, we establish an explicit benchmark to test whether the sampler recovers sample parameters. Evaluating 10 factors illustrates the scaling challenge where uniform grid search (‭\(10^{10}\)‬ points) becomes computationally impractical, while 250 observations preserve realistic parameter standard errors for downside modeling.

The Diagnostic Framework
In quantitative validation workflows, evaluating an MCMC sampler involves three core criteria: 1. Stationarity: The chain has converged to the target distribution and is invariant to initialization coordinates. 2. Mixing Across Dimensions: The chain traverses parameter space without prolonged freezing or sluggish diffusion. 3. Effective Sample Size (ESS): Autocorrelation decays rapidly enough to provide sufficient independent information for quantile estimation (Vehtari et al., 2021).

To evaluate convergence, four independent chains are run: one from \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^{(0)} = \mathbf{0}\) and three from overdispersed starting points at \(\pm 3\) posterior standard deviations from the posterior center (all high, all low, and mixed).

Diagnostic Review: Multi-Chain Trace and Split-\(\hat{R}\)
Four chains were run: one from \(\mathbf{0}\) and three from starting points \(\pm 3\) posterior standard deviations from the posterior center (all high, all low, and mixed). All 10 factors fail the \(\hat{R} < 1.01\) threshold, with a maximum split-\(\hat{R}\) of 1.057 (Tech Growth). US Treasuries sits exactly at the threshold.
The trace also shows that the 500-iteration burn-in is insufficient: Chain 3, started at \(-3\) posterior SDs, does not reach the posterior band until roughly iteration 700.
Chains started far apart have not fully mixed within 3,000 iterations, which is consistent with the low ESS reported below.



Autocorrelation Decay Analysis
Because Metropolis-Hastings operates via local proposals, consecutive draws exhibit positive serial dependence.


Code
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

calc_acf_df <- function(vec, factor_name, max_lag = 35) {
  res <- acf(vec, lag.max = max_lag, plot = FALSE)
  tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(res$lag),
    autocorrelation = as.numeric(res$acf),
    factor = factor_name
  )
}

acf_combined <- bind_rows(
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$Tech_Growth, "Tech Growth"),
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$US_Treas_10Y, "US Treasuries (10Y)"),
  calc_acf_df(draws1_clean$US_LargeCap, "US Large Cap")
)

ggplot(acf_combined, aes(x = lag, y = autocorrelation, fill = factor)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge", width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.10, linetype = "dashed", color = "#7f8c8d") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#2c3e50", "#2980b9", "#27ae60")) +
  labs(
    title = "Autocorrelation Decay by Factor",
    subtitle = "Autocorrelation decay profiles highlight the impact of isotropic proposal scaling on correlated parameters",
    x = "Lag Step",

Diagnostic Analysis: The Proposal-Geometry Mismatch
The autocorrelation profiles highlight an operational challenge when using an unscaled, isotropic proposal (‭\(\sigma_\epsilon \mathbf{I}\)‬‭‬) across correlated dimensions:

Treasuries (10Y): Autocorrelation decays quickly, dropping below 0.50 by lag 7 and reaching baseline levels near lag 20. With low return volatility (8%), the parameter space is compact.
Equity Beta (Tech Growth): Autocorrelation exhibits high persistence, remaining around 0.65 at lag 35. Because the scalar proposal step (‭\(\sigma_\epsilon = 0.00032\)‬‭‬) is applied identically across all dimensions, it does not account for the differing scales (Treasuries ‭\(\text{SE} \approx 0.03\%\)‬‭‬‭‬ vs. Tech ‭\(\text{SE} \approx 0.10\%\)‬‭‬‭‬) or the correlated geometry of the target density. As a result, the chain traverses the principal variance axes slowly, leading to persistent serial correlation.




Robust Effective Sample Size (ESS) Audit
To avoid truncation bias in persistent chains, Effective Sample Size is computed using Geyer’s initial sequence estimator across all post-burn draws:


Code
# Combine one factor's draws from all 4 chains into a 2,500 x 4 matrix
chain_matrix <- function(factor) {
  sapply(draws_clean, function(dc) dc[[factor]])
}

factors_audit <- c("Tech_Growth", "US_Treas_10Y", "US_LargeCap")

ess_pooled_bulk <- sapply(factors_audit, function(f)
  round(posterior::ess_bulk(chain_matrix(f))))
ess_pooled_tail <- sapply(factors_audit, function(f)
  round(posterior::ess_tail(chain_matrix(f))))

n_total <- nrow(draws1_clean) * length(draws_clean)   # 10,000


tibble(
  Asset_Class = c("Equity Beta (Tech Growth)", "Duration Hedge (10Y Treasuries)", "Core Market (US Large Cap)"),
  Total_Post_Burn_Draws = rep(nrow(draws1_clean), 3),

Pooled across all four chains (10000 draws), bulk ESS for Tech Growth is 65 and tail ESS is 132, still well below the recommended 400, consistent with the split-\(\hat{R}\) results above.
Model Validation Findings  A model validation review of the ESS diagnostics yields three key takeaways:

Sampling Efficiency Reflects Correlation Drag: Out of 2,500 post-burn iterations, Tech Growth yields only 16 effective independent draws, a sampling efficiency of 0.6%. Across the three audited factors, ESS ranges from 16 to 65. The acceptance rate of 28.9% falls within the conventional range, which shows that a healthy acceptance rate does not guarantee good mixing. The single, isotropic proposal step is too small for high-variance factors such as Tech Growth, so the chain crosses their posterior range slowly.
Independent Verification of the Estimator: ESS values from compute_ess_robust() (Geyer initial monotone sequence) were cross-checked against posterior::ess_basic(), which returned 14.5, 55.2, and 20.5 for Tech Growth, Treasuries, and US Large Cap. The two estimators agree closely. The reference package reads slightly lower because it uses split chains and a more conservative truncation rule.
Quantile Precision Considerations: Vehtari et al. (2021) recommend an ESS of at least 400 for reliable posterior summaries, and more for tail quantiles. Current ESS values of 16–65 fall well short. Even the posterior mean is imprecise: with an ESS of 16, the Monte Carlo standard error for Tech Growth is about 25% of a posterior standard deviation. The 5th and 95th percentiles that define the VaR and Expected Shortfall credible intervals are less stable still. The exact-posterior benchmark on the Portfolio Risk page shows the practical result: the MCMC credible intervals are too narrow, understating parameter risk.
Paths to Algorithmic Improvement: This diagnostic shows the trade-offs of first-principles isotropic Random-Walk Metropolis. In production risk environments, sampling efficiency can be improved by:

Proposal Covariance Preconditioning: Scaling jumps to the posterior geometry using \(\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{\text{prop}} = \frac{2.38^2}{d}\hat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}_{\text{post}}\) (Roberts & Rosenthal, 2001).
Adaptive Sampling: Adaptive Metropolis algorithms that learn the posterior covariance during the run (Haario et al., 2001).
Gradient-Based Methods: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) or NUTS, which use gradient information to move efficiently through high-dimensional, correlated posteriors.


See the exact-posterior benchmark on the Portfolio Risk page for the effect of low ESS on credible-interval width.
